html:
Around the late 9th or early 8th century BCE, Greeks took over the Phoenician alphabet and adapted it to their own language. The result, the Greek alphabet, was the first script to write vowels as well as consonants as a matter of course.

Phoenician traders sailed all over the Mediterranean, and Greeks met them in ports from Cyprus to the Levant coast. The Phoenician script had about 22 letters, all consonants. Greek needed vowels to be readable, so Greeks reused Phoenician letters for sounds their language did not have. The throat sound aleph became alpha, a vowel. The letter names stayed Semitic: alpha and beta come from aleph and beth, which is where the word "alphabet" comes from.

The earliest Greek inscriptions date to around 750 BCE. At first each region had its own version. Athens adopted the Ionic form in 403 BCE, and by the end of the 4th century BCE that 24-letter set was standard everywhere. It is still used today. Writing let the poems of Homer be fixed on the page.

Its children spread further:

  • A western Greek version, carried by colonists to Italy, passed to the Etruscans and from them to the Romans. It became the Latin alphabet.
  • In the 9th century CE, missionaries in the Balkans built the Cyrillic script largely on Greek letters.
sum: Around the late 9th or early 8th century BCE, Greeks took over the Phoenician alphabet and adapted it to their own language. The result, the Greek alphabet, was the first script to write vowels as well as consonants as a matter of course.
